Arleigh Kraus Warren LD 704
Arleigh A. Kraus March 3, 2025
LD704 An Act to Clarify Performance Standards for Quarries
Testimony in support of LD704
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation & Forestry. My name is Arleigh Kraus. I reside in Warren. I am a board member of Citizens Against Residential Mining Activities (CARMA). I am a small business owner and farmer as well as a policy consultant focused on marine debris removal of PFAS contaminated waste. I am testifying in support of LD704 a bill that would issue and improve quarrying standards for quarry operations using blasting. Currently several towns in Maine have quarry blasting occurring which is disruptive to the surrounding communities. The noise and concussion from explosions causes house foundations to crack, plaster to fall off of walls, furniture to fall and windows to shake. There are also instances of well casings cracking. The constant blasting is extremely loud and causes headaches and stress. The constant concussions also causes stress for animals. Regulations specific to times blasting is appropriate and strict adherence to a time schedule is absolutely necessary. We need to have in place specific agreements on when it is acceptable for blasting to occur for the safety and wellbeing of the community adjacent to quarries with blasting operations.
Thank you for your consideration. Respectfully, Arleigh Kraus

Representative Doudera, Senator Tepler, and the entire Environment and Natural Resources Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to present to you LD 704, "An Act to Clarify Performance Standards for Quarries." I am Bill Pluecker, and I represent House District 44 comprising the towns of Warren, Union, and Hope.
This past December I received a number of complaints about blasting in a gravel pit in Warren. Multiple families reported blasts knocking pictures off the walls and worries about windows being cracked. People reported hearing the blasts the next town over, in Thomaston, and called public safety to ensure that something awful had not happened.
I reached out to Deputy Commissioner Madore about the issue, and very much appreciated his prompt response to the issue. DEP staff conducted a site visit and reported that the blasting was the result of the construction of a 50' by 100' shop in the bottom of a gravel pit. While on site, they observed another small area drilled for another blast to happen on an unspecified date. DEP staff also confirmed that the building plan was approved by the town. The Deputy Commissioner informed me that excavations that are a part of a construction project are not regulated under the quarry law. Furthermore, DEP personnel concluded that the excavated area was less than one acre at the time of his site visit, meaning it was not subject to the Performance Standards for quarries. Since this project was not subject to Site Law and the excavation area was determined to be under one acre, it was not regulated under the quarry law.
After speaking to my town's code enforcement officer, it was clear that the volume of material that was blasted was quite valuable despite not being produced under existing site regulations, but was likely produced by taking advantage of a loophole

District 44: Hope, Union, & Warren

in the law that allows essentially unregulated blasting as long as construction on the site is permitted. I have heard stories that this is not a unique circumstance, and it is generally known that if a construction permit is obtained for a quarry, blasting can be conducted with much less review.
In my estimation, whether you are blasting in a quarry for the production of gravel or in order to install a foundation, it makes good sense that the same regulations would apply around notice to neighbors, appropriate timing of blasts, and noise reduction. In both situations, the site is the same, the neighbors are the same, and to a large degree, the production of gravel is similar and can be sold in both circumstances. I encourage you to pass this simple bill, and close this problematic loophole in the law.
Thank you very much. I apologize for not being able to make the hearing today. I am traveling with my aging parents, but I look forward to attending the work session to be able to discuss the bill with you further at that time. Please do not hesitate to reach out to me with any questions in the meantime.

Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Committee, my name is Rob Wood and I am the Director of the Bureau of Land Resources at the Department of Environmental Protection. I am speaking in opposition to L.D. 704. L.D. 704 would increase the scope of activities covered by the performance standards for quarries. The bill would require any quarry that employs blasting to meet the performance standards, regardless of the size of the quarry. The bill would also require any excavation or grading activity that involves blasting to meet the quarry performance standards, even if the activity is not part of a quarry. Blasting is common in a variety of construction projects, from construction of utility lines and roads to driveways and

The expanded coverage of the performance standards would result in substantially more construction projects that must submit a notice of intent to comply (N01) with the performance standards to the Department. The Department would be required to review the newly submitted NOIs and conduct compliance checks on sites to confirm the activities are meeting the performance standards. The Department's Mining Program does not currently have the staff resources necessary to implement this change.
The Department also notes that the Site Location of Development Law requires any blasting that occurs as part of a development licensed under the Site Law to meet the blasting standards applicable to quarry operations (see 38 M.R.S. �484(9)). If the purpose of L.D. 704 is to require all blasting activities to meet the blasting standards applicable to quarry operations (38 M.R.S. �490-Z(14)), many blasting activities at larger construction projects are already subject to these standards because they are subject to the Site Law.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify before you today. I would be happy to answer any questions from the Committee, both now and at the work session.
